AAPY: Options that mimic owning Apple stock, backed by Treasury bills and other bonds held as collateral. It sells options to pay regular income, which caps the gains when Apple climbs, so it is an income-first way to follow one giant technology stock.
ARVR: Companies building the metaverse: virtual worlds, gaming platforms, headsets and the chips and networks behind them, split between technology and media. Interest in the theme has cooled since its hype peak, so this is a contrarian growth bet that virtual worlds still become big business.
BBB: A fixed recipe in one fund: about three-quarters in the companies of the S&P 500 and one-quarter in bitcoin futures. The blend keeps most of a stock portfolio's growth while adding a permanent crypto slice, rebalanced back to the recipe, so bitcoin's wild swings are diluted but never absent.
BBLS: Seven large US energy companies dubbed the Munificent Seven, the oil and gas answer to the famous tech list. It is a concentrated bet on America's biggest energy names as a group, so it lives and dies with oil and gas prices and the seven firms' fortunes.
BPAY: Financial technology companies: payment networks, digital banks, trading platforms and the software behind them, split between finance and technology. It is a growth bet on money going digital, holding the disruptors rather than the old banks they are displacing.
CHRI: Companies from the S&P 500 screened to align with Christian moral and biblical teachings, which keeps the tech-heavy shape of the big index while removing names that fail the screen. It is a values-based core holding for faith-driven investors, accepting a somewhat narrower universe.
CMAG: The Magnificent Seven, the handful of mega-cap American tech giants that dominate the stock market, held in line with their market size. It is the market's most fashionable trade in one ticker: no diversification beyond seven names, so it rides entirely on big tech's fortunes.
CUST: US Treasury bonds with one to three years left until they come due, the short end of the government bond market. It is a low-risk income holding that pays more than cash or T-bills while moving only modestly when interest rates change.
DQSE: Options on the Nasdaq-100 arranged to gain from moves in either direction, rising when the market climbs and when it falls a little, over a period ending in September. In exchange it gives up gains beyond a cap, so it is a cushion holding for investors who cannot call tech's direction.
DWSH: An actively managed short fund that bets against US large-company stocks and stock funds, using relative-strength research to pick its targets. It is a bearish hedge designed to gain when the market falls, which also means steady losses in rising markets, so it suits short windows and hedges.
EPEM: Stocks from emerging markets around the world, heaviest in Asian technology: chipmakers, electronics manufacturers and internet companies, with banks and other industries behind them. It plays the growth role for developing economies, so it keeps those markets' currency swings, political risks and sharper ups and downs.
EUDV: European companies that have raised their dividends every year for at least a decade, spread across industry, health care, banking and materials. It is an income-and-quality holding for Europe, favoring dependable payers over the region's faster but riskier growers.
EZMO: A momentum system that holds US stock funds when markets look strong and shifts toward defense when its signals warn of decline. It is a rules-based attempt to dodge deep bear markets, which can work in long slumps but whipsaws when markets reverse quickly.
FLAO: Options on a US stock fund designed to put a floor under losses over six-month periods, with this series running April and October, in exchange for a cap on gains. The floor level is the one named in the fund's title, so the deal is limited downside for limited upside, reset twice a year.
FLJJ: Options on a US stock fund designed to put a floor under losses over six-month periods, with this series running January and July, in exchange for a cap on gains. The floor level is the one named in the fund's title, so the deal is limited downside for limited upside, reset twice a year.
GASZ: Companies that build and run natural gas power: turbine makers, plant builders and the infrastructure that feeds gas-fired generation. Data centers' hunger for reliable electricity is the story here, making it a focused bet on gas as the bridge fuel of the AI era.
GGRW: Companies tied to innovation across technology, industry, media and consumer brands, picked by a value-minded firm hunting for growth at reasonable prices. It is a thematic growth holding that tries to buy tomorrow's leaders before their prices fully reflect the story.
HAKY: Cybersecurity companies, the software and services firms that guard networks and data, paired with covered call options sold against the stocks. It trades some of a hot sector's upside for regular option income, aiming to smooth one of tech's jumpier themes.
HOLD: One dollar buys two strategies at once: about seventy-five cents of S&P 500 stocks plus a trend-following futures program of the same size layered on top. The futures layer trades bonds, currencies and commodities long and short, aiming to help most in long market declines, at the cost of extra complexity.
HWIV: Undervalued companies outside the US, in developed and emerging markets alike, picked by a deep-value firm across banking, technology, industry and materials. It plays the patient value role abroad, buying profitable firms when they are out of favor and waiting for the market to come around.
IBGB: US Treasury bonds that mature in 2045, held in a fund designed to wind up at the end of that year. Long-dated government bonds are the most rate-sensitive of all, so this is a date-targeted holding that can swing hard long before its final year arrives.
JDOC: Health care leaders across drugmakers, biotech, medical devices, services and health technology, picked where the managers think future growth is underappreciated. It is a focused bet on medicine's biggest franchises, more concentrated than a broad health fund and driven by drug pipelines and trial results.
KNOW: A global mix of stocks and a smaller slice of bonds, bought on fundamental value and held for the long term with little trading. It plays the all-in-one portfolio role with a moderately aggressive tilt, letting the managers' patience and stock selection drive results.
LJUL: Treasury bills plus options on the S&P 500 that pay an income stream while absorbing the first slice of market losses named in the fund's title. It is built for investors who want stock-market-linked income with a cushion, trading away most upside and renewing its terms each period, with this series starting in July.
LYLD: Large US companies returning the most cash to shareholders through dividends, buybacks and debt repayment combined, a measure called shareholder yield. Cambria's model favors these cash-returning firms, which tilts the fund toward banks and energy and away from growth stocks that reinvest everything.
MCDS: Mid-sized US companies chosen by blending traditional analyst research with data science, spread across technology, industry, banking and health care. It plays the core mid-cap role with a quantitative edge, aiming for the middle of the market where growth and stability meet.
MLDR: US Treasury bonds arranged as a ladder, with money spread evenly across maturities from three to ten years, refreshed each year. Laddering balances yield against safety: some bonds are always near maturity, softening rate swings, making it a steady intermediate government bond holding.
MOTO: Companies reinventing how people and goods move: electric and self-driving vehicles, connected-car technology and ride and delivery services. It is a global growth bet on cleaner, smarter transport, spread between carmakers, chip firms and industrial suppliers.
MYCM: Corporate bonds from US companies that mostly come due in 2033, held as a date-targeted income portfolio. It suits money aimed at a goal around 2033: interest payments along the way, company credit risk throughout, and rate risk that fades as the due dates approach.
MYCN: Corporate bonds from US companies that mostly come due in 2034, held as a date-targeted income portfolio. It suits money aimed at a goal around 2034: interest payments along the way, company credit risk throughout, and rate risk that fades as the due dates approach.
MYMF: Municipal bonds from US states and cities that mostly come due in 2026, paying interest that is exempt from regular federal income tax. It suits savers aiming at a goal around 2026, with tax-free income along the way and risk that eases as the bonds near their due dates.
MYMG: Municipal bonds from US states and cities that mostly come due in 2027, paying interest that is exempt from regular federal income tax. It suits savers aiming at a goal around 2027, with tax-free income along the way and risk that eases as the bonds near their due dates.
PMDE: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb as much loss as the structure allows over a one-year period ending in December, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is the most defensive version of a buffer fund, suiting investors who fear a down year more than they want full upside.
PRAM: Two linked corners of the chip world: memory makers, whose chips store the data AI chews through, and photonics firms that move it with light. It is a deep-tech bet on the plumbing of artificial intelligence, more specialized than broad semiconductor funds and just as cyclical.
SATO: Companies in the crypto economy, miners, exchanges and technology enablers, plus a slice held directly in bitcoin and ether products. It offers crypto exposure through the stock market, so it swings with coin prices while adding the business risks of young, thinly traded companies.
SCDS: Small US companies chosen by blending traditional analyst research with data science, spread across health care, banking, technology and industry. It plays the core small-cap role with a quantitative edge, aiming to own the steadier earners among small stocks rather than the whole speculative pack.
SETH: A trading tool that bets against ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, aiming to gain each day that its price falls. It uses futures and resets daily, so longer results drift from a simple mirror image, making it a short-term hedge for crypto holders rather than an investment.
SLVX: Silver miners and refiners, paired with options on silver companies and funds that turn the metal's swings into income. Silver pays no dividend on its own, so the options program manufactures payouts, while the price still rides a metal known for violent moves.
SOLC: Direct ownership of SOL, the Solana blockchain's token, with the holdings staked through the Marinade protocol to earn extra tokens. Staking adds a yield on top of the price, paid in more of the same coin, so returns rise and fall with both Solana's price and its network rewards.
SPCK: Blank-check SPAC companies hunting for businesses to buy, plus companies that went public within the last two years. It is an event-driven bet on deal-making and fresh listings, where early hype can lift prices fast and disappointing deals can sink them just as quickly.
TBJL: Options on the big fund of 20-year Treasury bonds, built to absorb the first 9% of losses over a period ending in July, the buffer level in its name. Long bonds swing the most when rates move, so this trades some upside for a softer landing when rates jump.
TCAN: The CC token of the Canton Network, a blockchain built for banks and financial firms to trade and settle assets with privacy controls. It is a single-cryptocurrency fund on a young, institution-focused network, so the price can swing wildly on thin trading and adoption news.
THRV: A multi-asset income portfolio built mostly from other funds: bond funds, closed-end funds, dividend stocks and some commodities, chosen for their payouts. It aims to pay steady income from many sources at once, accepting the extra layer of fees and complexity that fund-of-funds structures bring.
TSNF: US companies at the frontiers of innovation, across artificial intelligence, biotechnology, space, defense technology and other next-generation industries. It is a growth bet on tomorrow's headline sectors today, concentrated in technology and health care, with the sharp swings of young themes.
UTWY: A single holding: the most recently issued 20-year US Treasury bond, replaced as new bonds are auctioned. Twenty-year bonds are among the most rate-sensitive investments available, so this precise building block can swing hard even though the borrower is the US government.
VNIE: Companies outside the US, spread across at least three countries, with technology, industry and banking the biggest groups. It is an actively managed foreign growth holding from a Swiss firm known for quality stock picking, adding currency swings to the usual market risk.
WTMU: Municipal bonds from US states and cities arranged in a ladder, with bonds coming due at staggered dates across the intermediate years. Interest is generally free of federal income tax, and the ladder balances income against rate risk, a classic core muni holding for taxable accounts.
XSHP: Exposure to a single private company, SpaceX, gained through derivatives and any shares available, backed by bonds, with options sold to add income. SpaceX does not trade on an exchange, so this is a rare public route to it, with extra layers of cost and guesswork in valuing a private firm.
YSPY: An income strategy built on options tied to a triple-leveraged S&P 500 fund rather than on the index itself. It sells options to harvest the huge premiums a 3-times fund creates, aiming for large payouts while taking amplified losses in a market slide, since the underlying resets its leverage daily.
ZINC: Income-producing US stocks picked for their payouts, leaning on banks, utilities, food and household staples and energy companies. It is a value-flavored income holding, favoring steady dividend payers over growth, so it should hold up better in flat markets and trail in tech-led rallies.
